road.text: A rear derailleur has to move a turning chain onto any one of eleven cogs, using nothing but one cable. The biggest cog wraps about seventy-three millimetres more chain than the smallest, and the chain is a fixed length, so the cage pays out chain as the chain climbs the cassette and takes it back as the chain drops.

It bolts to the hanger on the frame. Below that, a parallelogram of two links and four pins swings sideways: the cable pulls it one way, and a return spring pulls it back. At the bottom, the cage carries two small pulleys. The guide pulley steers the chain onto a cog, and the tension pulley keeps it tight.

One click of the shifter pulls 2.67 millimetres of cable. The parallelogram moves the pulley 1.4 times as far, so the guide pulley moves exactly one cog: 3.74 millimetres. The turning chain follows it onto the next cog.

A cable can only pull. Click the other way, and the shifter lets the cable out, so the return spring pulls the parallelogram back out. The return spring does the work, and the chain drops to the smaller cog.

But the chain only moves while it turns. Only forward pedalling drives the chain, so coasting and backpedalling do not shift. With the pedals still, the pulley moves at once and the chain just runs at an angle. Pedal, and a ramp and pin on the next cog come round, catch the chain's plate and lift it across.

Now the chain climbs to the twenty-eight. The bigger cog takes chain from the loop through the cage, about forty-seven millimetres of it, and most of the rest from the lower run to the chainring. The cage spring only ever turns the cage back, taking up slack; so it is the chain's pull on the tension pulley that turns the cage about sixty degrees forward, winding the spring tighter.

Three screws set the limits. The H screw stops the parallelogram on the smallest cog's line, so a slack cable and the return spring can't throw the chain off outboard into the dropout. The L screw does the same on the largest, so a tight cable or a knock can't throw the chain into the spokes. The B screw turns the whole derailleur about its mounting bolt, which moves the guide pulley toward or away from every cog together. Set it with the chain on the largest cog, as close as it can run without touching. Too close, and the guide pulley's teeth reach the largest cog's; too far, and the chain crosses a longer unsupported run to the big cogs.

Cables stretch and housings settle. If the cable runs just one millimetre slack, every cog but the smallest lands 1.4 millimetres outboard of its cog. The smallest is held on its line by the H screw and the return spring. So if the chain hesitates or rubs going up to a larger cog, the cable is slack, so turn the barrel adjuster out, counter-clockwise, to take it up. If the downshift hesitates or the chain rubs the next larger cog, the cable is tight, so turn it in, clockwise. Make the final adjustment while pedalling, trying every gear.
